title: Leadership and teamwork within a project
apm_learning_objective: Understand leadership and teamwork within a project.
exam_coverage_note: 4 outcomes. Worth 4 marks normally, but 10.4 names two models, so this objective is a strong candidate for the outcome the handbook says is assessed twice.
source_ref: APM PFQ Qualification Handbook, APM-QS-PFQ-8 V5 (April 2026), §11d. Syllabus maps this objective to APM Body of Knowledge 7th ed. 3.1.3, 3.2.1, 3.2.3, 3.2.4 and 8th ed. 4.1, 4.3, 4.3.1, 4.3.3, 4.4, 4.4.1, 4.4.2, 4.4.3.
competence_area_note: The handbook publishes no per-objective Competence Framework mapping. Left null rather than guessed.
where_this_fits: The last objective, and the one where the syllabus stops describing processes and starts describing people. Four outcomes, and the final one names two models, Belbin and Tuckman, so both need learning properly rather than one of them.

key_definitions.definition: The ability to establish vision and direction, and to influence and align others towards a common purpose.
key_definitions.plain_english: Getting people to want to go somewhere, rather than instructing them to.

key_definitions.definition: The planning, organising and controlling of resources and activities to achieve defined objectives.
key_definitions.plain_english: Making sure the work happens properly. Related to leadership, and not the same thing.

key_definitions.definition: A model of team development describing the stages of forming, storming, norming and performing.
key_definitions.plain_english: The predictable stages a new team goes through before it works well.

key_definitions.definition: A model describing the behavioural roles individuals adopt in teams, used to understand team balance.
key_definitions.plain_english: The different parts people naturally play in a team, and why a team of nine identical people struggles.

key_definitions.definition: A team whose members are located in different places, working across distance and often across time zones.
key_definitions.plain_english: A team that does not share a room, and often does not share a working day.

core_content.key_takeaway: Leadership is the ability to establish vision and direction, and to influence and align others towards a common purpose. It is not formal authority and it is not a job title. Authority is granted by position and can compel compliance, while leadership works through influence and produces commitment.
core_content.body_markdown:
Four components sit in the definition and the exam draws on all of them: vision, direction, influence, alignment.

The critical point is what leadership is not. Project managers commonly have to lead people they have no authority over, particularly where team members report to a line manager elsewhere. That is exactly why the distinction from authority matters in practice and not only in the exam.

Leadership is also distinct from management, though the two go together. Management plans, organises and controls the work. Leadership sets direction and brings people with you. A project needs both, and a project manager is normally doing both at once.

core_content.outcome_title: Explain how a project team leader can influence team performance
core_content.key_takeaway: A project team leader influences performance through clarity of role and objective, trust and openness so that bad news arrives early, routine feedback rather than saved up feedback, recognition of contribution, and involving people in decisions so that they commit to them. The leader's own behaviour also sets the standard the team follows.
core_content.body_markdown:
A small number of things consistently matter.

Clarity of role and objective comes first. People who know exactly what they are responsible for, and what the team is trying to achieve, perform better than people working it out as they go. Ambiguity produces both gaps and duplication.

Trust and openness follow. A team that can raise bad news early is a team whose leader hears about problems while they are still small. A team that cannot will present a green status report until the week the project fails.

Feedback given routinely, rather than saved up, lets people correct course while correcting is still cheap.

Recognition sustains effort, particularly on long projects where the end feels distant.

And the leader's own behaviour sets the standard. A leader who conceals problems has a team that conceals problems, whatever the stated policy says.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline the challenges to a project manager when developing and leading a project team
core_content.key_takeaway: The challenges are that team membership is temporary and changing, that authority is often incomplete because members also report to a line manager, that teams are frequently dispersed across locations and time zones, that skills and working styles vary because the team is assembled from whoever was available, that conflict arises from competing priorities and resource pressure, and that the work itself carries deadlines, uncertainty and change. Co-location is not a challenge, because it removes several of these.
core_content.body_markdown:
Project teams are harder to lead than permanent ones, for reasons that follow from what a project is.

Membership is temporary and changing. People join and leave as the project moves through its phases, so the team is repeatedly re-forming.

Authority is often incomplete. Team members may report to a line manager as well as to the project, so the project manager can carry responsibility without formal authority.

Dispersal across locations and time zones reduces non-verbal signal and makes disengagement and conflict harder to spot.

Skills, experience and working styles vary, because a project team is usually assembled from whoever was available rather than selected for balance.

Conflict comes from competing priorities, personality differences and resource pressure, and has to be handled rather than avoided.

And the work itself carries deadlines, uncertainty and change, all of which land on the same people.

One thing that is not a challenge is co-location. Having the team in one place removes several of the problems above, and it turns up in exam options as the odd one out.

core_content.outcome_title: Outline how a project manager can use models to assist team development
core_content.key_takeaway: Tuckman describes the stages a team passes through: forming, the tentative beginning where roles are unclear; storming, where members challenge roles and each other and productivity often dips; norming, where roles settle and trust develops; and performing, where the team delivers effectively with little intervention. Belbin describes the behavioural roles people adopt within a team, such as the plant who generates ideas, the implementer who turns them into action and the completer finisher who checks the detail, and a project manager uses it to get a balanced mix and spot the gaps.
core_content.body_markdown:
Tuckman's model describes how a team develops.

Forming is the polite, tentative beginning. Members are getting oriented, roles are unclear, and the leader is directive because nobody yet knows how the team works.

Storming is the conflict stage. Members challenge roles, approaches and each other, and productivity often dips. This is normal and necessary rather than a sign of failure, and a leader who suppresses it usually finds the same disagreements resurfacing later and less openly.

Norming is where roles settle, working practices are agreed and trust develops.

Performing is effective delivery, where the team works with little intervention and the leader can step back.

The practical use is setting expectations. A project manager who knows storming is coming reads early conflict as a stage rather than a crisis. And because project teams change membership, a team that gains or loses people can go back to an earlier stage.

Belbin's model describes the behavioural roles people adopt within a team, grouped broadly into action oriented, people oriented and thinking oriented roles. The plant generates ideas, the implementer turns them into action, the completer finisher checks the detail, the coordinator draws contributions out of others, and the resource investigator looks outside the team for opportunities.

The practical use is balance. A team of nine idea generators produces no delivery, and a team with no idea generator produces nothing new.

misconceptions.wrong: Leadership and management are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: Management plans, organises and controls the work. Leadership sets direction and aligns people towards it. Projects need both, usually from the same person.

misconceptions.wrong: You need formal authority to lead.
misconceptions.right: Leadership works through influence. Project managers routinely lead people who report elsewhere, which is why influence rather than authority is in the definition.

misconceptions.wrong: Storming means the team has gone wrong.
misconceptions.right: It is a normal and necessary stage. Suppressing it tends to push the same disagreements underground, where they surface later and cost more.

misconceptions.wrong: Once a team reaches performing, it stays there.
misconceptions.right: Project teams change membership constantly, and a team that gains or loses people can revisit earlier stages.

misconceptions.wrong: Belbin's model is about personality types.
misconceptions.right: It describes behavioural roles people adopt in a team context. Its use is understanding balance and gaps, not labelling individuals permanently.

misconceptions.wrong: Co-locating the team is a challenge to be managed.
misconceptions.right: Co-location removes several challenges. It is dispersal that creates difficulty, and co-location is the standard odd-one-out in exam lists.

misconceptions.wrong: Avoiding conflict keeps a team productive.
misconceptions.right: Unaddressed conflict does not disappear. Openness and early feedback are what let a leader deal with it while it is still small.

memory_aids.expansion: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing. Tuckman's four stages in order. Polite, then fighting, then settled, then effective.
Tuckman is stages a team moves through. Belbin is roles people play within it. One is time, the other is composition.
Any option defining leadership as formal power over a team is wrong.
In a list of team challenges, look for the item that is actually a help. It is usually co-location or stable membership, and it kills every option containing it.

progress_checkpoint: I can define leadership using vision, direction, influence and alignment.
I can explain the difference between leadership and formal authority.
I can name five things a team leader does that improve team performance.
I can list five genuine challenges of leading a project team, and spot the item in a list that is actually a benefit.
I can name Tuckman's four stages in order, describe the behaviour at each, and explain why storming is normal.
I can say what Belbin's model describes and how a project manager uses it.

source_confidence.claim: The two named team development models are Belbin and Tuckman.
source_confidence.basis: Named in the bracketed 'including' list in syllabus outcome 10.4. The handbook states bracketed content is examinable.

source_confidence.claim: Outcome 10.4 is a strong candidate for the outcome assessed twice.
source_confidence.basis: In the published 2022 sample paper, 10.4 is the only outcome appearing twice, once for Belbin and once for Tuckman. All other 58 outcomes appear once.
source_confidence.risk: One observation from one paper. The handbook states that one outcome is assessed twice but never says which, and it may vary between sittings. Teach both models thoroughly; do not tell learners to expect two questions here.

source_confidence.claim: Tuckman's model has four stages for PFQ purposes.
source_confidence.basis: Forming, storming, norming and performing are the stages tested in the sample paper and referenced by the syllabus.
source_confidence.risk: Tuckman later added a fifth stage, adjourning. It is not required at PFQ level and is omitted deliberately to keep the recall load on what is examinable.
